media-pipeline — Configuration API

Rust · Windows · Native Capture Pipeline

Configuring Pipeline with custom settings

Resolution, frame rate, video bitrate, audio bitrate, capture source, recording, and streaming — all set through one PipelineConfig before you call start().

01 The shape of a config

Everything the pipeline does is decided up front by the PipelineConfig you hand to Pipeline::new. Video settings are required; recording, streaming, and audio are each opt-in.

use media_pipeline::{
    Pipeline, PipelineConfig, RecordConfig, StreamConfig,
    AudioConfig, VideoConfig, CaptureTarget,
};

let config = PipelineConfig {
    // what to capture
    capture_target: CaptureTarget::Monitor(0),
    capture_cursor: true,

    // custom video settings
    video: VideoConfig {
        width: 2560,
        height: 1440,
        fps: 60,
        bitrate: 12_000_000,        // 12 Mbps
        keyframe_interval: 120,     // 2s GOP at 60 fps
    },

    // record to disk (None to disable)
    record: Some(RecordConfig {
        output_path: "capture.mp4".into(),
    }),

    // stream to RTMP (None to disable)
    stream: Some(StreamConfig {
        url: "rtmp://live.example.com/app".into(),
        stream_key: "your-stream-key".into(),
    }),

    // custom audio settings (None for video-only)
    audio: Some(AudioConfig {
        loopback: true,        // system / desktop audio
        microphone: true,      // default mic (skipped if absent)
        bitrate: 192_000,      // 192 kbps AAC
    }),
};

let mut pipeline = Pipeline::new(config)?;
pipeline.start().await?;
// ... running ...
pipeline.stop().await?;
Note

start() and stop() are async so they drop straight into a #[tauri::command], but the capture and encode work runs on its own OS thread — it never blocks the async runtime. start() returns once the pipeline is live; is_recording() and is_streaming() reflect state immediately after.

02 Video settings

The VideoConfig fields control resolution, frame rate, and the H.264 encoder. Implements Default, so you can override just the fields you care about.

FieldTypeDefaultWhat it does
widthu321920 Encoded frame width in pixels. Set to your capture resolution (e.g. 3840 for 4K).
heightu321080 Encoded frame height in pixels (e.g. 2160 for 4K).
fpsu3230 Target frame rate. Drives per-frame timestamps and pacing. 30 or 60 are typical.
bitrateu326_000_000 Average target video bitrate in bits per second. Higher = better quality, larger files, more bandwidth.
keyframe_intervalu3260 GOP size in frames between keyframes. Keep short for streaming — a late viewer waits up to this long for a keyframe to start decoding.

Override only what you need

// start from defaults, change three fields
let video = VideoConfig {
    width: 3840,
    height: 2160,
    fps: 60,
    ..VideoConfig::default()
};
Constraint

Use even dimensions. H.264 (4:2:0) and the RTMP/FLV path expect even width and height. Odd values can fail encoder negotiation. Set keyframe_interval to roughly 2 × fps for streaming so viewers and network segments align on a ~2-second keyframe cadence.

4K note

At 3840×2160 the v1 software encoder does a per-frame GPU→CPU copy plus a CPU H.264 encode and may not keep up at 30 fps. The hardware zero-copy path is the intended 4K route — see the encoder notes in the crate.

03 Audio settings

Set audio to Some(AudioConfig { .. }) to capture sound, or None for video-only. Recording writes system audio and microphone as two separate AAC tracks; streaming publishes a single mixed AAC track.

FieldTypeDefaultWhat it does
loopbackbooltrue Capture system / desktop audio via WASAPI loopback (game and app sound).
microphonebooltrue Capture the default input device. Silently skipped if no microphone exists.
bitrateu32128_000 AAC bitrate in bits per second. 128 kbps is transparent for most content; 192–256 kbps for music. 
// system audio only, higher bitrate for a music stream
let audio = AudioConfig {
    loopback: true,
    microphone: false,
    bitrate: 256_000,
};
Routing

Sample rate and channel count are read from the device (commonly 48 kHz stereo) — you set the bitrate, the pipeline matches the format. In the MP4, loopback is track 0 and mic is track 1. For RTMP, both sources are summed into one track since FLV carries a single audio stream.

04 Capture source & outputs

What to capture

CaptureTarget selects the source. The index or window handle is yours to supply.

CaptureTarget::Monitor(0)          // monitor by index (0 = first enumerated)
CaptureTarget::Window(hwnd)         // a specific window, HWND as isize

capture_cursor: bool toggles whether the mouse cursor is drawn into the frame.

Recording, streaming, or both

  • record: Some(RecordConfig { output_path }) — write an MP4. output_path is any Into<PathBuf> (a &str works).
  • stream: Some(StreamConfig { url, stream_key }) — publish over RTMP. url is the ingest URL up to the app (e.g. rtmp://host:1935/live); stream_key is the stream name that follows.
  • Set either to None to disable that branch. At least one must be enabled, or Pipeline::new returns an error.
One encode

When both are on, the frame is encoded once and forked to both outputs — recording never drops a frame, while the stream may drop non-keyframes under network backpressure (never a keyframe).

// 1080p60 streaming preset, expanded
PipelineConfig {
    capture_target: CaptureTarget::Monitor(0),
    capture_cursor: true,
    video: VideoConfig {
        width: 1920, height: 1080, fps: 60,
        bitrate: 6_000_000, keyframe_interval: 120,
    },
    record: None,
    stream: Some(StreamConfig {
        url: "rtmp://localhost:1935/live".into(),
        stream_key: "test".into(),
    }),
    audio: Some(AudioConfig {
        loopback: true, microphone: true, bitrate: 160_000,
    }),
}

Fields, types, and defaults reflect the current public API in media-pipeline (PipelineConfig, VideoConfig, AudioConfig, RecordConfig, StreamConfig, CaptureTarget). Bitrates are in bits per second; keyframe interval is in frames.
